questions.subject: Christian Religious Studies
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how examples and analogies relate professed faith to conduct.
questions.prompt: In James 2:15–17, what makes the speaker’s farewell inadequate? Explain how the example supports the argument about faith.
questions.answer: The needy person still lacks food and clothing. A verbal wish does not provide either, so the example exposes the gap between a profession of concern and conduct that gives it effect.
questions.explanation: The argument uses a specific unmet need to illustrate the inadequacy of faith claimed without deeds.

markingGuide.description: Explain why the words are insufficient.
Connect the example to professed faith.

questions.subject: Christian Religious Studies
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how examples and analogies relate professed faith to conduct.
questions.prompt: Compare the functions of the examples of demons and Rahab in James 2. What does each contribute to the argument?
questions.answer: The demons show that correct recognition of God can coexist with a lack of faithful conduct. Rahab’s reception and protection of the messengers gives a positive example of faith expressed through action.
questions.explanation: The two examples make contrasting contributions. One limits what assent demonstrates, while the other illustrates action.

markingGuide.description: Explain the example of the demons.
Identify what Rahab does for the messengers.
Explain the contrast in argumentative function.

questions.subject: Christian Religious Studies
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how examples and analogies relate professed faith to conduct.
questions.prompt: What is the function of the body-and-spirit comparison at the end of James 2?
questions.answer: It illustrates why faith without deeds is described as dead.
questions.explanation: James uses the lifeless body as an analogy for faith separated from deeds.
options: It explains why material assistance is unnecessary.
It illustrates why faith without deeds is described as dead.
It introduces a distinction between rich and poor worshippers.
It establishes that only spoken promises are evidence of faith.

questions.subject: Christian Religious Studies
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how examples and analogies relate professed faith to conduct.
questions.prompt: A reader says that Abraham’s action in James 2 is described as unrelated to his prior faith. Which response best fits the passage?
questions.answer: James presents the faith as working with the action and reaching fulfilment through it.
questions.explanation: James 2:22 directly connects the faith and action. The relationship is central to the example.
options: James presents the faith as working with the action and reaching fulfilment through it.
James treats Abraham’s action as evidence that Abraham had never believed.
James describes the action as unrelated to anything Abraham believed.
James introduces Abraham solely to discuss the treatment of wealthy visitors.

questions.subject: Christian Religious Studies
questions.learningObjective: Analyse James’s account of favouritism and apply its reasoning to comparable situations.
questions.prompt: At a youth fellowship, two first-time visitors arrive together. An organiser moves one to a better seat solely because their clothes look expensive. Explain how James 2:1–4 would evaluate the decision and give a fair seating rule.
questions.answer: The organiser assigns honour on the basis of apparent wealth, resembling the favouritism James criticises. The group could use a consistent arrival-order rule with accommodations for access needs.
questions.explanation: Apply the passage’s objection to status-based preference and explain how the proposed rule avoids that criterion.

markingGuide.description: Connect it to the seating contrast in James.
Give a feasible rule that avoids favouring apparent wealth.

questions.subject: Christian Religious Studies
questions.learningObjective: Analyse James’s account of favouritism and apply its reasoning to comparable situations.
questions.prompt: A group argues that giving extra honour to a wealthy visitor is harmless because its members obey several other moral commands. Assess that defence using James 2:8–11.
questions.answer: James treats loving one’s neighbour as a governing obligation and identifies partiality as a breach. He argues that obedience elsewhere does not erase disobedience to a command of the same lawgiver. The group’s other conduct therefore does not excuse the discriminatory act.
questions.explanation: The defence attempts to offset one breach with other acts of obedience. The passage addresses responsibility for the breach itself.

markingGuide.description: State a judgement on the defence.
Explain the neighbour-love principle and its relation to partiality.
Explain why obedience elsewhere does not cancel the breach.

questions.subject: Christian Religious Studies
questions.learningObjective: Analyse James’s account of favouritism and apply its reasoning to comparable situations.
questions.prompt: In James 2:1–4, what difference in treatment makes the seating incident an example of partiality?
questions.answer: The visitor who appears wealthy receives the more honoured place.
questions.explanation: James contrasts the invitation given to the finely dressed visitor with the instruction given to the poor visitor.
options: Both visitors are invited to take the same place.
The visitor arriving first chooses a seat.
The visitor who appears wealthy receives the more honoured place.
Both visitors are directed to stand for the same reason.

questions.subject: Christian Religious Studies
questions.learningObjective: Analyse James’s account of favouritism and apply its reasoning to comparable situations.
questions.prompt: Which principle does James explicitly name when arguing against favouritism in James 2:8–9?
questions.explanation: James invokes neighbour-love and then explains that showing partiality violates the law.
options: Repay each gift with an equal gift.
Reserve public honour for those who contribute most.
Avoid speaking to anyone whose status is unknown.
